query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A carefully trained machine-learning (ML) interatomic potential, fitted to a representative set of ab initio solid and liquid snapshots for a chosen multi-component high-entropy alloy, will reproduce ab initio–level free energies and derived fusion properties (e.g., melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion) at a fraction of the computational cost compared to direct first-principles molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD calculations.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic (or near-equiatomic) high-entropy alloy samples in both solid and liquid states near the melting transition.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an ML-based potential (e.g., neural network or Gaussian process) trained on sparse but carefully selected ab initio data encompassing relevant compositions and high temperatures. Then perform large-scale molecular-dynamics simulations with the trained potential to calculate solid and liquid free energies (including vibrational entropy and electron–vibration coupling).
generation.conditions: Temperatures spanning approximately ±10% around the expected melting range, for a broad set of representative compositions of high-entropy alloys containing four or more principal elements.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential’s local structural descriptors capturing anharmonic vibrational modes and atomic interactions in both the solid and molten phases.
generation.mechanism: Once trained on ab initio data from diverse snapshots spanning the relevant phase space, the ML model estimates energies and forces with near first-principles fidelity, enabling extensive and efficient sampling of phase-space configurations in both solid and fluid regimes.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML-driven approach will predict fusion thermodynamics (melting temperatures, enthalpies of fusion, phase diagrams) within approximately 1–2% of the results from explicit ab initio simulations, while attaining at least an order-of-magnitude speedup relative to TOR-TILD for high-entropy systems.
generation.baseline: Direct ab initio molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD free-energy workflows currently required for elemental/binary and extended to quaternary/quinary alloys.
generation.boundary: Accuracy depends on the quality and diversity of the ab initio training set. Extrapolation beyond trained compositional and temperature ranges may introduce errors, requiring additional data and retraining for new regimes.
generation.uncertainty: If the ML model’s training set does not capture relevant defect environments, complex phase transformations, or electron–vibration coupled states, the method’s predictive accuracy may degrade. Model hyperparameter choices and representational capacity can also limit performance.

falsification_experiment.design: For a chosen high-entropy alloy composition, ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations and TOR-TILD reference calculations are performed at multiple temperatures around the expected melting transition to generate reference free-energy data. In parallel, an ML interatomic potential is trained on a judiciously chosen subset of these simulations. The ML potential is then used to calculate free energies, melting curves, and derived fusion properties (enthalpies of fusion, entropy changes). Cross-compare ML-based predictions with both ab initio/TOR-TILD computations (in the training range and slightly beyond) and available experimental measurements of fusion properties.
measurements: Free energies of coexisting solid and liquid phases
Melting temperatures derived from the constructed phase diagram
Enthalpies of fusion obtained by thermodynamic integration or coexistence simulations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-predicted free energies or derived fusion properties deviate from ab initio or experimental data by more than ~2% or fail to identify the correct melting transition, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. We investigate the phase stability of the solid-solution phase of the metallic Al x CrCoFeNi alloys ( x = 0.0 – 2.0 mole-fraction) using the Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) Green’s function method in combination with the screened Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [37] [38] . The scalar-relativistic approximation is used for the valence electrons (no spin-orbit terms). The exchange-correlation functionals used are the von Barth-Hedin [39] local density approximation (LDA) as parameterized by Moruzzi, Janak, and Williams [40] and generalized gradient approximation (GGA) by Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof revised for solids (PBEsol) [41] . A variational definition [42] of the potential zero (v 0 ) is utilized to yield the kinetic energies and dispersion that approach those of full-potential methods [42] [43] . Potentials, charge densities, and total energies are obtained, using a complex-energy Gauss-Legendre semicircular contour with 24 points, and Brillioun-zone integrations use a special k-point method [44] with a 20 × 20 × 20 mesh. decision.trend: Across refractory and high-temperature HEAs such as Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 and NbMoCrTiAl (studied in PMC5578249 and PMC7513042), early work focused on experimental approaches to characterize microstructure, mechanical strength, creep resistance, and oxidation or irradiation tolerance. These studies established that high-entropy alloys can outperform conventional alloys at elevated temperatures but did not comprehensively address free-energy evaluations at or near the melting point. Research on W-based HEAs for fusion-relevant environments (PMC6397024) revealed the promise of multi-component systems to resist irradiation damage, again focusing on experimental and partial theoretical methods rather than full free-energy modeling. More recently, first-principles calculations (PMC11375712) have mainly been employed to understand electronic and magnetic properties, but remain prohibitively expensive for large or compositionally complex HEAs when evaluating free energies across both solid and liquid phases with full vibrational and electronic contributions. Consequently, a reliable, high-throughput computational strategy for capturing fusion properties, including fusion enthalpies, is still missing for multi-component alloys.
decision.unsolved: The main unresolved hurdle is reducing the computational cost of first-principles methods that accurately capture free energies (solid and liquid) with vibrational entropy, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration coupling. While techniques like TOR-TILD have shown success for simpler systems, they become computationally prohibitive for high-entropy systems with four or more elements. A robust, generalizable, and scalable approach is not yet established for efficient, high-fidelity free-energy determination in such complex alloys.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning-based interatomic potential (e.g., a neural network or Gaussian process model) trained on a sparse set of ab initio calculations for carefully chosen solid and liquid snapshots, ensuring coverage of the compositional and high-temperature range near the melting point. Then use this ML potential to run large-scale molecular dynamics simulations that include anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling in the free-energy evaluation.
decision.why: A properly trained ML potential can reproduce ab initio accuracy at a fraction of the cost, enabling exhaustive sampling of both solid and molten states in complex multicomponent systems. This approach has shown success in simpler binary systems and can be extended to high-entropy alloys. It will be orders of magnitude faster than direct ab initio MD or TOR-TILD, and it preserves relevant entropic contributions if the training set ensures broad configuration diversity. A decisive benchmark would compare ML-based free energies, melting temperatures, and derived properties (e.g., heat capacity and enthalpy of fusion) against those obtained from smaller-scale, fully ab initio simulations and, where possible, experimental measurements of fusion properties. Any significant disagreement in phase boundaries, melting behavior, or thermodynamic observables would falsify the hypothesis.
